name: Specialist Knowledge Repository (K_C)
description: Category-specific knowledge K_c = {F_c, D_c} with D_c = {T_c, M_c, I_c} (common targets, specialised techniques, distinctive indicators) per Definition 1.

Credential Theft.definition: Counterfeit interfaces that impersonate legitimate platforms in order to capture user authentication credentials for account takeover.
primary_features: Password field, or an email-first login flow that leads to one.
Brand-locked sign-in card that accepts credentials for a single impersonated provider.
Multi-provider webmail chooser routing every brand to the same form.
'Stay signed in', 'Forgot password' and 'Create account' affordances copied from the target.
Second-factor prompt: OTP, authenticator code, SMS PIN, security question.
common_targets: Email providers: Outlook, Office365, Gmail, Yahoo, Zimbra, RoundCube, cPanel webmail.
Banking and net-banking portals, and their corporate cash-management logins.
Social platforms: Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X, WeChat.
Enterprise SSO: Microsoft 365, Okta, Google Workspace, VPN and Citrix gateways.
Cloud storage: OneDrive, SharePoint, Dropbox, Google Drive, Adobe Document Cloud.
Telecom and ISP self-care portals; gaming launchers; crypto exchanges.
techniques: Credential harvesting form posting to an attacker-controlled PHP handler or Telegram bot.
Two-stage flow: password first, then OTP, to defeat SMS-based MFA in real time.
Pre-filled victim email address passed through the URL to increase credibility.
Document-lure gating: a blurred invoice or shared file behind a sign-in wall.
Fake error 'incorrect password' on first submit to capture the credential twice.
Obfuscated or base64-encoded page source and cloaking against security crawlers.
indicators: Any visible password input is the single strongest indicator of this category.
'Sign in', 'Log in', 'Continue', 'Verify your account' as the primary call to action.
Account-security framing: 'unusual activity', 'session expired', 'confirm it is you'.
Provider logo above a minimal two-field form with no other site functionality.
Domain in the screenshot unrelated to the brand whose login is displayed.
counter_indicators: A real password manager or browser-native dialog rather than an in-page form.
A registration form that collects profile data but no authentication secret.

Financial Fraud.definition: Pages engineered for direct monetary exploitation - payment-instrument capture or solicitation of a transfer.
primary_features: Card number, expiry, CVV/CVC or cardholder-name fields.
Explicit amount due, fee, fine, customs charge or subscription price.
Payment-network branding: Visa, Mastercard, JCB, 3-D Secure, Verified by Visa, J/Secure.
Bank transfer instructions, UPI/IBAN details or crypto wallet address and QR code.
Investment return promises, refund forms, or 'claim your prize' payout flows.
common_targets: Banking and card customers; online shoppers at checkout.
Parcel recipients charged a small 'redelivery' or customs fee.
Crypto investors and wallet holders; subscription renewals and streaming services.
techniques: Small-amount lure (a 1-3 unit fee) to make card entry feel low-risk.
Fake 3-D Secure interstitial that harvests the one-time payment code.
Advance-fee framing: pay a processing charge to release a larger sum.
Technical-support scam demanding payment for a fabricated infection.
Wallet-drain approval disguised as an airdrop claim or token migration.
Countdown timers on the payment screen to prevent verification.
indicators: CVV or expiry-date field present - a legitimate login never requires these.
Currency symbols and an itemised amount adjacent to a submission button.
'Pay now', 'Confirm payment', 'Release funds', 'Claim refund' calls to action.
Card-art imagery or payment-network logo strip beneath the form.
Unrealistic yield, guaranteed-profit or lottery-win messaging.
counter_indicators: A product catalogue with no payment capture on the visible page.
Donation or pricing information that is purely descriptive.

Malware Distribution.definition: Deceptive interfaces that induce the visitor to execute or install a malicious payload.
primary_features: Prominent download button or auto-started download notification.
Software-update, codec, media-player or PDF-reader impersonation.
Simulated antivirus scan reporting infections and offering a 'cleaner' tool.
Instructions to disable protection, allow notifications, or run a command.
Browser-extension or mobile APK install prompt from a non-official store.
common_targets: Users seeking free software, cracks, media files or document viewers.
Visitors alarmed by fake system or browser security warnings.
Corporate users receiving 'required update' notices for common tooling.
techniques: Fake CAPTCHA that instructs the user to paste a command into a run dialog.
Drive-by download chained to a redirect from an ad or shortened link.
Archive password given on the page so the payload evades scanning.
Extension bait: 'install this plugin to view the document'.
Repeated overlay pop-ups that make the download the only escape path.
indicators: 'Download', 'Install', 'Update now', 'Start download', 'Get the app' buttons.
File names, sizes or extensions (.exe, .apk, .dmg, .zip, .scr) shown on screen.
Red or yellow alarm imagery with scan progress and threat counts.
Version badges or 'your player is out of date' messaging.
Instruction steps numbered 1-2-3 that end in running a file.
counter_indicators: A legitimate product page where the download is the site's genuine purpose.
A document preview with no executable delivery path.

Personal Information Harvesting.definition: Collection of personally identifiable information well beyond authentication secrets, enabling identity theft or resale.
primary_features: Full name, date of birth, residential address, postcode fields.
National identifiers: SSN, Aadhaar, NRIC, passport, driving licence, tax ID.
Phone number, alternate email, mother's maiden name or other recovery data.
Employment, income, health, insurance or education details.
Document or selfie upload controls for 'identity verification' / KYC.
common_targets: Benefit, tax-refund, subsidy and grant claimants.
Delivery recipients asked to 'confirm' their address details.
Healthcare, insurance and telecom customers completing 'verification'.
techniques: Progressive profiling across multiple steps so no single page looks excessive.
Survey or quiz framing with a reward at the end.
KYC or age-verification pretext requiring an ID photo.
Address-confirmation step appended after a credential capture page.
Optional-looking fields that are in fact mandatory to proceed.
indicators: Three or more distinct PII fields visible on one form.
Asterisk-marked mandatory fields for identity data on a consumer page.
Labels such as 'Delivery address', 'ID number', 'Date of birth', 'Occupation'.
Upload controls beside identity-document wording.
Data requested is disproportionate to the stated purpose of the page.
counter_indicators: A login page that only asks for an email address as the account identifier.
A checkout shipping form on a genuine merchant site.

co_occurrence_notes: Credential Theft + Personal Information Harvesting is the dominant pair: the page takes the password and then 'verifies' identity with address and phone.
Credential Theft + Financial Fraud appears when a banking login is immediately followed by card or transfer capture.
Financial Fraud + Personal Information Harvesting occurs on refund, fine and customs-fee pages that need both card and identity data.
Malware Distribution rarely co-occurs; when it does it is usually with Credential Theft on fake software-portal logins.
Assign multiple labels only when distinct evidence supports each one - not because a category is plausible.
